claim: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a leading cause of invasive disease in infants, especially in low-income settings.
source: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a leading cause of invasive disease in infants, especially in low-income settings.
evidence: This is a general statement about disease burden that draws from established scientific knowledge about pneumococcal disease epidemiology.

claim: Asymptomatic carriage in the nasopharynx is a prerequisite for disease.
source: Asymptomatic carriage in the nasopharynx is a prerequisite for disease, but variability in its duration is currently only understood at the serotype level.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about pneumococcal pathogenesis.

claim: Variability in carriage duration is currently only understood at the serotype level.
source: Asymptomatic carriage in the nasopharynx is a prerequisite for disease, but variability in its duration is currently only understood at the serotype level.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature in the introduction and represents the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: Pneumococcal genomic variation accounted for 63% of the phenotype variation in carriage duration.
source: We estimated that pneumococcal genomic variation accounted for 63% of the phenotype variation, whereas the host traits considered here (age and previous carriage) accounted for less than 5%.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the heritability analysis performed in the study using the ANOVA-CPP method.

claim: Host traits (age and previous carriage) accounted for less than 5% of phenotype variation in carriage duration.
source: We estimated that pneumococcal genomic variation accounted for 63% of the phenotype variation, whereas the host traits considered here (age and previous carriage) accounted for less than 5%.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the regression analysis of host factors.

claim: Serotype accounts for 17% of variation in carriage duration.
source: We further partitioned this heritability into both lineage and locus effects, and quantified the amount attributable to the largest sources of variation in carriage duration: serotype (17%), drug-resistance (9%) and other significant locus effects (7%).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the variance partitioning analysis.

claim: Drug-resistance accounts for 9% of variation in carriage duration.
source: We further partitioned this heritability into both lineage and locus effects, and quantified the amount attributable to the largest sources of variation in carriage duration: serotype (17%), drug-resistance (9%) and other significant locus effects (7%).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the variance partitioning analysis.

claim: Other significant locus effects account for 7% of variation in carriage duration.
source: We further partitioned this heritability into both lineage and locus effects, and quantified the amount attributable to the largest sources of variation in carriage duration: serotype (17%), drug-resistance (9%) and other significant locus effects (7%).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the GWAS analysis.

claim: Prophage sequences are associated with decreased carriage duration independent of serotype.
source: A pan-genome-wide association study identified prophage sequences as being associated with decreased carriage duration independent of serotype, potentially by disruption of the competence mechanism.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the GWAS analysis using linear mixed models.

claim: Prophage sequences may decrease carriage duration by disrupting the competence mechanism.
source: A pan-genome-wide association study identified prophage sequences as being associated with decreased carriage duration independent of serotype, potentially by disruption of the competence mechanism.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the association findings based on the comYC analysis.

claim: Pneumococcal disease burden is highest in children.
source: Pneumococcal disease burden is highest in children (O'Brien et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Understanding and predicting the amount of time pneumococci spend in the nasopharynx is critical for understanding this bacterium's epidemiology and controlling transmission.
source: The pneumococcus spends most of the transmission cycle in the nasopharynx, and so understanding and predicting the amount of time spent in this niche is critical for understanding this bacterium's epidemiology, and therefore controlling transmission (Abdullahi et al., 2012a; Melegaro et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Serotype strongly associates with carriage duration.
source: One factor that is known to strongly associate with carriage duration is serotype: as capsular polysaccharides are important in bacterial physiology and determining host immune response, different serotypes have different clearance and acquisition rates (Abdullahi et al., 2012a; Hill et al., 2010; Högberg et al., 2007; Melegaro et al., 2004; Turner et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Different serotypes have different clearance and acquisition rates.
source: One factor that is known to strongly associate with carriage duration is serotype: as capsular polysaccharides are important in bacterial physiology and determining host immune response, different serotypes have different clearance and acquisition rates (Abdullahi et al., 2012a; Hill et al., 2010; Högberg et al., 2007; Melegaro et al., 2004; Turner et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Changes in average carriage duration have been shown to be linked with recombination rate.
source: Changes in average carriage duration have been shown to be linked with recombination rate (Chaguza et al., 2016), which has been found to correlate with antibiotic resistance (Hanage et al., 2009) and invasive potential (Chaguza et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Recombination rate has been found to correlate with antibiotic resistance.
source: Changes in average carriage duration have been shown to be linked with recombination rate (Chaguza et al., 2016), which has been found to correlate with antibiotic resistance (Hanage et al., 2009) and invasive potential (Chaguza et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Recombination rate has been found to correlate with invasive potential.
source: Changes in average carriage duration have been shown to be linked with recombination rate (Chaguza et al., 2016), which has been found to correlate with antibiotic resistance (Hanage et al., 2009) and invasive potential (Chaguza et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Carriage duration by different serotypes is widely used in models of pneumococcal epidemiology.
source: The carriage duration by different serotypes is widely used in models of pneumococcal epidemiology, and consequently is important in evaluating the efficacy of the pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV) (Melegaro et al., 2007; Weinberger et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Modelling work has proposed that if alleles exist which alter carriage duration, these explain how antibiotic-resistant and sensitive strains stably coexist in the population.
source: Additionally, modelling work has proposed that if alleles exist which alter carriage duration, these explain the long standing puzzle of how antibiotic-resistant and sensitive strains stably coexist in the population (Lehtinen et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The study population consisted of 598 unvaccinated children with up to 24 swabs taken over a two year period.
source: For 598 unvaccinated children up to 24 swabs taken over a two year period were available, an extension on the previous study (Turner et al., 2012, 2013a).
evidence: This describes the study design and data collection.

claim: Only swabs from infants were considered because mothers did not have sufficient sampling resolution relative to their average length of carriage.
source: We only considered swabs from infants in the study, as mothers did not have sufficient sampling resolution relative to their average length of carriage to determine carriage duration.
evidence: This explains a methodological decision based on data characteristics.

claim: The immune response of mothers to bacterial pathogens is different to children, leading to shorter carriage durations.
source: Furthermore, the immune response of mothers to bacterial pathogens is different to children (Maródi, 2006), leading to shorter carriage durations (Gritzfeld et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A total of 4382 carriage episodes were estimated (7.3 per child).
source: From all the swab data, we estimated that there were a total of 4382 carriage episodes (7.3 per child), of which 2254 had a complete set of AMR data available (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the HMM analysis of swab data.

claim: 2254 carriage episodes had a complete set of AMR data available.
source: From all the swab data, we estimated that there were a total of 4382 carriage episodes (7.3 per child), of which 2254 had a complete set of AMR data available (Figure 3).
evidence: This describes the data available for analysis.

claim: 2157 sequenced genomes were matched with a carriage duration after removing outliers.
source: After removing ten outlier observations from swabs taken accidentally during disease, we were able to match 2157 sequenced genomes with a carriage duration.
evidence: This describes the final dataset used for genetic analysis.

claim: The genetics of S. pneumoniae is an important factor in determining carriage duration in this population.
source: This implies that the genetics of S. pneumoniae is an important factor in determining carriage duration in this population.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the high heritability estimate.

claim: The total variance explained by serotype and resistance lineage factors was 0.19.
source: The total variance explained by these lineage factors was 0.19, 0.178 for serotype alone and 0.092 for resistance alone.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the lasso regression analysis.

claim: Serotype alone explained 0.178 of variance in carriage duration.
source: The total variance explained by these lineage factors was 0.19, 0.178 for serotype alone and 0.092 for resistance alone.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the lasso regression analysis.

claim: Resistance alone explained 0.092 of variance in carriage duration.
source: The total variance explained by these lineage factors was 0.19, 0.178 for serotype alone and 0.092 for resistance alone.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the lasso regression analysis.

claim: 19F serotype caused significant increase in carriage duration.
source: We applied the covariance test (Lockhart et al., 2014) to determine which lineage effects were significantly associated with carriage duration and found that 19F, erythromycin resistance, 23F, 6B caused significant (α<0.05) increase in carriage duration and being non-typable caused a significant decrease.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the covariance test on lasso regression results.

claim: Erythromycin resistance caused significant increase in carriage duration.
source: We applied the covariance test (Lockhart et al., 2014) to determine which lineage effects were significantly associated with carriage duration and found that 19F, erythromycin resistance, 23F, 6B caused significant (α<0.05) increase in carriage duration and being non-typable caused a significant decrease.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the covariance test on lasso regression results.

claim: 23F serotype caused significant increase in carriage duration.
source: We applied the covariance test (Lockhart et al., 2014) to determine which lineage effects were significantly associated with carriage duration and found that 19F, erythromycin resistance, 23F, 6B caused significant (α<0.05) increase in carriage duration and being non-typable caused a significant decrease.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the covariance test on lasso regression results.

claim: 6B serotype caused significant increase in carriage duration.
source: We applied the covariance test (Lockhart et al., 2014) to determine which lineage effects were significantly associated with carriage duration and found that 19F, erythromycin resistance, 23F, 6B caused significant (α<0.05) increase in carriage duration and being non-typable caused a significant decrease.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the covariance test on lasso regression results.

claim: Being non-typable caused a significant decrease in carriage duration.
source: We applied the covariance test (Lockhart et al., 2014) to determine which lineage effects were significantly associated with carriage duration and found that 19F, erythromycin resistance, 23F, 6B caused significant (α<0.05) increase in carriage duration and being non-typable caused a significant decrease.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the covariance test on lasso regression results.

claim: No significant difference in duration was seen between isolates with or without capsule within the same lineage (p=0.39).
source: No significant difference in duration was seen between isolates with or without capsule within the same lineage (p=0.39; Figure 4).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the analysis of capsule gain/loss events.

claim: The main lineage effect on carriage duration is the serotype, but only some serotypes (19F) have an association independent of genetic background.
source: Together, this suggests that the main lineage effect on carriage duration is the serotype, but only some serotypes (19F) have an association independent of genetic background.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from multiple analyses including lasso regression and LMM.

claim: Erythromycin resistance may be significantly associated with an increased carriage duration.
source: We also found that erythromycin resistance may be significantly associated with an increased carriage duration.
evidence: This is a finding from the lasso regression and covariance test.

claim: The majority of carriage episodes were due to five of the seven paediatric serotypes or non-typeable isolates.
source: The majority of carriage episodes were due to five of the seven paediatric serotypes (Shapiro and Austrian, 1994), or non-typeable isolates.
evidence: This is a finding from the HMM analysis and descriptive statistics.

claim: 19F, 23F and 14 were carried the longest.
source: The results show 19F, 23F and 14 were carried the longest, 6A/C and 6B for intermediate lengths, and NT the shortest.
evidence: This is a finding from the HMM analysis of mean sojourn times.

claim: 6A/C and 6B were carried for intermediate lengths.
source: The results show 19F, 23F and 14 were carried the longest, 6A/C and 6B for intermediate lengths, and NT the shortest.
evidence: This is a finding from the HMM analysis of mean sojourn times.

claim: NT (non-typeable) pneumococci were carried the shortest.
source: The results show 19F, 23F and 14 were carried the longest, 6A/C and 6B for intermediate lengths, and NT the shortest.
evidence: This is a finding from the HMM analysis of mean sojourn times.

claim: The overall picture of the first two years of infant carriage is one containing one or two long (over 90 day) carriage episodes of a common serotype and around two short (under a month) carriage episodes of non-typable S. pneumoniae.
source: The overall picture of the first two years of infant carriage is one containing one or two long (over 90 day) carriage episodes of a common serotype (6A/C, 6B, 14, 19F, 23F) and around two short (under a month) carriage episodes of non-typable S. pneumoniae.
evidence: This is a summary inference from the HMM analysis results.

claim: The only genome-wide significant SNP hits are synonymous changes (MAF = 1%) in the replication module of the prophage.
source: The only genome-wide significant SNP hits are synonymous changes (MAF = 1%) in the replication module of the prophage in the ATCC 700669 genome (Croucher et al., 2009), a highly variable component of the pneumococcal genome (Croucher et al., 2014a) (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the GWAS analysis with annotation.

claim: The most significant k-mer hits were located in phage sequence (MAF 2%) and were associated with a reduced duration of carriage.
source: The most significant k-mer hits were also located in phage sequence (MAF 2%) and were associated with a reduced duration of carriage.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the k-mer GWAS analysis.

claim: No evidence of association was found between presence of any phage in the genome and carriage duration when correcting for population structure (p=0.35).
source: By using the presence of phage as a trait under the same linear mixed model, we however found no evidence of association when correcting for population structure (p=0.35).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the LMM analysis of phage presence.

claim: Infection with a specific phage sequence is associated with a slight decrease in carriage duration.
source: These results are therefore evidence that infection with a specific phage sequence is associated with a slight decrease in carriage duration.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the GWAS results showing specific phage sequences but not general phage presence associated with carriage duration.

claim: A similar result has previously been found in Neisseria meningitidis, where a specific phage sequence was found to affect the virulence and epidemiology of strains.
source: A similar result has previously been found in a genome-wide screen in Neisseria meningitidis, where a specific phage sequence was found to affect the virulence and epidemiology of strains (Bille et al., 2005; Bille et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Previous in vivo tests have shown phage elements to cause a fitness decrease of S. pneumoniae during carriage.
source: Additionally, previous in vivo tests have shown phage elements to cause a fitness decrease of S. pneumoniae during carriage (DeBardeleben et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The effect of phage k-mers may be through interrupting comYC.
source: An interpretation consistent with these findings would be that the effect of phage k-mers is actually through interrupting comYC.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the association findings.

claim: Age and previous carriage together explained 0.046 of variation in carriage duration.
source: Together, they explained 0.046 of variation in carriage duration.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the regression analysis.

claim: Increasing child age contributes to a decrease in the duration of carriage episodes.
source: As found previously, increasing child age contributes to a decrease in the duration of carriage episodes.
evidence: This is a finding from the regression analysis, consistent with previous studies.

claim: From a mean of 68 days long, carriage duration drops 19 days after a year, and 32 days after two years.
source: From a mean of 68 days long, we calculated a drop of 19 days after a year, and 32 days after two years.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the regression analysis of age effects.

claim: Extrapolating, carriage episodes longer than two days cease by age 11.
source: Extrapolating, this causes carriage episodes longer than two days to cease by age 11 (Figure 6).
evidence: This is an extrapolation from the regression model shown in Figure 6.

claim: Previous carriage of any serotype was estimated to cause an increase in the duration of future carriage episodes.
source: Previous carriage of any serotype was estimated to cause an increase in the duration of future carriage episodes, though previous studies have found no overall effect (Weinberger et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a finding from the regression analysis, though it contradicts previous studies.

claim: The positive effect of previous carriage is likely to be an artefact due to subsequent carriage episodes being more likely to be due to typable pneumococci.
source: The positive effect observed in this analysis is therefore likely to be an artefact due to subsequent carriage episodes being more likely to be due to typable pneumococci.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the finding based on previous observations in the cohort.

claim: Sequence variation of the pneumococcal genome explains most of the variability in carriage duration (63%) despite other factors such as host age.
source: We found that despite a range of other factors such as host age which are known to cause carriage duration to differ, sequence variation of the pneumococcal genome explains most of this variability (63%).
evidence: This is a summary of the heritability findings.

claim: Common serotypes and resistance to erythromycin cause 19% of the effect on carriage duration.
source: Common serotypes and resistance to erythromycin cause some of this effect (19% total), as does the presence or absence of particular prophage sequence in the genome.
evidence: This is a summary of the variance partitioning findings.

claim: The presence or absence of particular prophage sequence in the genome affects carriage duration.
source: Common serotypes and resistance to erythromycin cause some of this effect (19% total), as does the presence or absence of particular prophage sequence in the genome.
evidence: This is a summary of the GWAS findings.

claim: Variants other than serotype affect carriage duration, consistent with recent theoretical work.
source: Importantly, our analysis of heritability shows that variants other than serotype affect carriage duration, consistent with recent theoretical work (Lehtinen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference from the heritability analysis, supported by citation to theoretical work.

claim: Variants exist in the pneumococcal genome which alter carriage duration, which in turn is linked to antibiotic resistance.
source: Together these studies suggest that variants exist in the pneumococcal genome which alter carriage duration, which in turn is linked to antibiotic resistance.
evidence: This is an inference combining the current findings with previous theoretical work.

claim: The close association of the phenotype with lineage limited power to fine-map lineage associated variants other than capsule type which may affect carriage duration.
source: The close association of the phenotype with lineage limited our power to fine-map lineage associated variants other than capsule type which may affect carriage duration.
evidence: This is a discussion of the limitations of the study based on the observed data structure.

claim: The study population was a subset of infants from the Maela longitudinal birth cohort.
source: The study population was a subset of infants from the Maela longitudinal birth cohort (Turner et al., 2013a), and was split into two cohorts.
evidence: This describes the study design and population.

claim: In the 'routine' cohort, 364 infants were swabbed monthly from birth, 24 times in total.
source: In the 'routine' cohort, 364 infants were swabbed monthly from birth, 24 times in total.
evidence: This describes the study design for one cohort.

claim: In the 'immunology' cohort 234 infants were swabbed on the same time schedule.
source: In the 'immunology' cohort 234 infants were swabbed on the same time schedule, but cultured and serotyped following the World Health Organisation (WHO) method (Turner et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the study design for the second cohort.

claim: 3161 randomly selected pneumococcal positive swabs from the study population have been previously sequenced.
source: 3161 randomly selected pneumococcal positive swabs from the study population have been previously sequenced, 2175 of which were from these longitudinal infant samples (Chewapreecha et al., 2014a).
evidence: This describes the genomic data available, citing previous work.

claim: 2175 of the sequenced swabs were from longitudinal infant samples.
source: 3161 randomly selected pneumococcal positive swabs from the study population have been previously sequenced, 2175 of which were from these longitudinal infant samples (Chewapreecha et al., 2014a).
evidence: This describes the genomic data available for the current analysis.

claim: The models for 19F, 23F, 6A/C, 6B, 14 and non-typable (NT) converged.
source: The models for 19F, 23F, 6A/C, 6B, 14 and non-typable (NT) converged, but other serotypes did not have enough observations to successfully fit the parameters of the model.
evidence: This describes the results of the HMM fitting process.

claim: Other serotypes did not have enough observations to successfully fit the parameters of the HMM model.
source: The models for 19F, 23F, 6A/C, 6B, 14 and non-typable (NT) converged, but other serotypes did not have enough observations to successfully fit the parameters of the model.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the HMM fitting process.

claim: At 1% proportional abundance in the sample, 12% of non-typable S. pneumoniae came out as culture negative.
source: At 1% proportional abundance in the sample, 12% came out as culture negative (Table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the 16S sequencing analysis used to calibrate the false negative rate.

claim: Based on having >1% abundance of 16S reads showing the bacteria as being present, 44/361 true positive swabs were not successfully cultured.
source: Based on having >1% abundance of 16S reads showing the bacteria as being present, 44/361 true positive swabs were not successfully cultured.
evidence: This is data from Table 1 showing the false negative rate of culture.
